sections.title: Measuring the magnitude of a force
The Force of Friction: Often Overlooked but Always Present
Forces Acting on a System of Objects

slides.title: Measuring Force with a Spring Balance
slides.kicker: How big is your push, really?
bullets: A spring balance measures the weight of objects and the magnitude of any force in general.
Pull the free end of the balance and it reads the force with which you pull on the spring inside.
Weight itself is the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls the object.
slides.note: One instrument, many forces. Handy na?

slides.title: The Everyday Force Scale
slides.kicker: The smallest push you can feel
bullets: In everyday life, the smallest forces we can directly feel are of the order of millinewtons (10^-3 N).
A light touch on your skin is a good example of such a small, directly felt force.

slides.title: Scientists Measure the Invisible
bullets: Scientists can measure forces far smaller than anything we feel, down to yoctonewtons (10^-24 N) in specialised experiments (as of 2026).
That is 10^21 times smaller than the millinewton forces of a light touch.

slides.title: Forces Rarely Act Alone
slides.kicker: Look closer, there is always company
bullets: Push a box placed on a surface and two forces act: your push forward and the force of friction backward.
A ball floating on water feels the gravitational force pulling it down and the buoyant force of the liquid pushing it up.

slides.title: Balanced Forces Hold Still
bullets: In tug of war, if both teams pull the rope with equal force, the rope does not move.
Forces that are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction are called balanced forces.
The rope moves only when one team pulls harder, making the forces unbalanced.
slides.note: Equal and opposite, so kuch nahi hota!

slides.title: Net Force Decides Motion
bullets: When opposite forces are unequal, the net force equals the difference of their magnitudes and points along the larger force.
When two forces act in the same direction, the net force is their sum, pointing that same way.
Example 6.1: forces of 10 N and 6 N give a net force of 16 N together or 4 N against each other.

items: Net points along the larger force
Object moves with the net force

slides.title: Friction, the Silent Blocker
bullets: A box on the floor does not move until your push beats the friction between its bottom surface and the floor.
Friction acts in a direction opposite to the force you apply.
The box starts moving only when your force is larger than friction, so a net force acts in the direction of motion.
slides.note: Friction is the strict teacher of motion!

slides.title: Every Force on a Box
bullets: Besides your push and friction, the box feels its weight downward and the normal force from the surface upward.
The normal force acts upward, perpendicular to the surface, and the two vertical forces are balanced.
Air also exerts friction on a moving box, but in many cases it is so small that we neglect it.

slides.title: Why You Must Keep Pushing
bullets: Stop pedalling a bicycle and it slows down and comes to rest after travelling some distance.
Friction acts against the direction of motion, so a continuous force is needed to keep an object moving.
The force of friction also depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact.

slides.title: Newton's First Law
bullets: An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues with constant velocity, unless a net force acts upon it.
If the net force is zero, the body cannot begin to move or change its velocity, so its acceleration is zero.
Constant velocity means no change in magnitude or direction, so non-zero constant velocity is straight-line motion.
slides.note: Objects bhi aaram pasand karte hain!

slides.title: Equal Push, Steady Motion
bullets: A person pushes a moving box forward with a force exactly equal to the friction between the box and the floor.
The two forces are equal and opposite, so they balance and the net force is zero.
By the first law, the box continues moving with constant velocity instead of coming to rest.

slides.title: Graphs with No Net Force
bullets: An object at rest keeps the same position with time, and its velocity stays zero.
An object moving with constant velocity gives a straight position-time graph and a flat velocity-time graph.

slides.title: Force Makes Things Accelerate
bullets: A ball pushed gently starts moving slowly from rest, so the acceleration due to your force is small.
A strong push makes it start moving fast, so a larger force gives a larger acceleration.
Hypothesis for the same object: a larger force results in a larger acceleration.

slides.title: The Cart and Pulley Test
bullets: A cardboard cart on ball-bearing wheels is pulled by a thread running over a small pipe used as a pulley.
The falling cup pulls the thread, and the thread pulls the cart with a constant force.
Weights of different magnitudes in the cup apply forces of different magnitudes to the same cart.

slides.title: Second Law, Clearly Stated
bullets: Newton's second law: when a net force acts on an object, the object accelerates in the direction of the net force.
The acceleration is found from the net force divided by the mass: a = F/m.
So the same force on a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration.
slides.note: Bhaari cheez ko hilana mushkil hai!

slides.title: Forces Always Come Paired
bullets: Kick a ball with your foot and you feel a force applied by the ball back on your foot.
Push a table away while sitting on a wheeled chair and your chair rolls in the opposite direction.
Each time you apply a force on the table, the table applies a force on you in the opposite direction.

slides.title: Push Ground, Move Forward
bullets: On a bicycle, push the ground backward with your feet and both you and the bicycle move forward.
The ground applies a force on your feet in the opposite direction, pushing you ahead.
Walking and running work the same way: your feet push the ground backward.

slides.title: When Friction Becomes a Friend
slides.kicker: Grip is friction working for you
bullets: The forward force from the ground while walking is friction, so here friction helps you move rather than oppose you.
Grooves on the soles of footwear and treads on tyres increase the force of friction with the floor and the road.
Without enough friction your foot slips backward, which is why wet polished floors are difficult to walk on.

slides.title: Two Boxes, One String
bullets: Two boxes of masses m1 and m2 rest on a frictionless horizontal surface, connected by a string.
A force F pulls Box 1 to the right, and Box 1 applies a force on Box 2 through the string.
By Newton's third law, Box 2 applies an equal and opposite force on Box 1; this string force is called tension T.

slides.title: Internal versus External Forces
bullets: Tension acts between the boxes inside the system, so it is an internal force.
The pull F acts from outside the system, so it is an external force.
Only forces that act from the outside matter for how the whole system accelerates.

slides.title: One System, One Acceleration
bullets: Treat the two boxes and the string as a single system, like one object of mass m1 + m2.
Newton's second law then gives the acceleration of the system: a = F/(m1 + m2).
Vertically, the gravitational force (m1g + m2g) is balanced by the normal force (N1 + N2) from the ground.

flashcards.front: Which instrument can measure the magnitude of any force, not just weight?
flashcards.back: A spring balance. Pulling its free end shows the force with which you pull on the spring inside.

flashcards.front: What is the weight of an object?
flashcards.back: The gravitational force with which the Earth pulls the object.

flashcards.front: What is the size of the smallest forces we directly feel in daily life?
flashcards.back: Forces of the order of millinewtons (10^-3 N), like a light touch.

flashcards.front: How tiny a force can scientists measure, as of 2026?
flashcards.back: Down to yoctonewtons (10^-24 N) in specialised experiments.

flashcards.front: When are two forces said to be balanced?
flashcards.back: When they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so the object does not move.

flashcards.front: How do you find the net force of two opposite, unequal forces?
flashcards.back: Subtract the magnitudes; the net force points along the force of larger magnitude.

flashcards.front: Two people push a stalled car in the same direction. What is the net force?
flashcards.back: The sum of the magnitudes of both forces, acting in that same direction.

flashcards.front: A ball floats still on water. Which two forces balance it?
flashcards.back: The gravitational force pulling down and the buoyant force of the liquid pushing up.

flashcards.front: In which direction does friction act on a pushed box?
flashcards.back: Opposite to the direction of the applied force and of the motion.

flashcards.front: When will a pushed box finally start moving?
flashcards.back: When your applied force is larger than the force of friction, so a net force acts forward.

flashcards.front: What is the normal force?
flashcards.back: The force a surface exerts on an object placed on it, upward and perpendicular to the surface.

flashcards.front: State Newton's first law of motion.
flashcards.back: An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues with constant velocity, unless a net force acts upon it.

flashcards.front: If the net force on an object is zero, what is its acceleration?
flashcards.back: Zero. The body cannot begin to move or change its velocity in magnitude or direction.

flashcards.front: You push a moving box forward exactly as hard as friction pulls back. What happens?
flashcards.back: The forces balance, the net force is zero, so the box keeps moving with constant velocity.

flashcards.front: What does a net force do to an object's velocity?
flashcards.back: It produces acceleration, which changes the velocity of the object.

flashcards.front: In the cart activity, what pulls the cart with a constant force?
flashcards.back: The thread, pulled by the falling cup and the weights inside it.

flashcards.front: How are net force, mass and acceleration linked in Newton's second law?
flashcards.back: a = F/m. Acceleration grows with the net force and shrinks with the mass.

flashcards.front: When you push a table while sitting on a wheeled chair, what do you feel?
flashcards.back: The table applies a force on you in the opposite direction, so your chair rolls away.

flashcards.front: While walking, which force actually pushes you forward?
flashcards.back: Friction from the ground, acting forward when your foot pushes the ground backward.

flashcards.front: Why do soles have grooves and tyres have treads?
flashcards.back: To increase the force of friction between soles or tyres and the ground for a better grip.

flashcards.front: In the two-box system, why is tension called an internal force?
flashcards.back: It acts between parts of the system itself, so it need not be considered for the system as a whole.

flashcards.front: Acceleration of two boxes (m1, m2) pulled by force F on a frictionless surface?
flashcards.back: a = F/(m1 + m2); the system accelerates like a single object of mass m1 + m2.

flashcards.front: Which outside forces act on the two-box system besides the pull F?
flashcards.back: The gravitational force (m1g + m2g) downward, balanced by the normal force (N1 + N2) upward.

quiz.q: Which instrument measures the magnitude of a force in general, not just the weight of an object?
quiz.why: A spring balance reads weight and, when you pull its free end, the magnitude of any force.

quiz.q: The weight of an object is which force?
options: The gravitational force with which the Earth pulls the object
The push of air on the object
The friction from the ground below
The buoyant force of water around it
quiz.why: The book defines weight as the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls the object.

quiz.q: As of 2026, the smallest forces measured in specialised experiments are of the order of
quiz.why: Scientists can measure forces down to yoctonewtons (10^-24 N) in specialised experiments.

quiz.q: In tug of war, both teams pull the rope with equal force in opposite directions. The rope
options: Moves in both directions at once
quiz.why: Equal and opposite forces are balanced, so the rope does not move.

quiz.q: Forces of 10 N and 6 N act on a block in opposite directions. The net force is
quiz.why: Opposite unequal forces subtract; the net force points along the larger 10 N force.

quiz.q: Two forces of 10 N and 6 N act on a block in the same direction. The net force is
quiz.why: Forces in the same direction add up: 10 N + 6 N = 16 N.

quiz.q: A box rests on the floor. You push it forward but it does not move. Why?
options: Friction from the floor balances your push
quiz.why: Friction acts opposite your push; the box moves only when your force exceeds friction.

quiz.q: For a box resting on a table, which force acts upward, perpendicular to the surface?
quiz.why: The normal force is exerted by the surface, upward and perpendicular to it, balancing the weight.

quiz.q: You stop pedalling a bicycle. Why does it finally come to rest?
options: No force ever acted on it
Friction acted against its motion all along
quiz.why: Friction acts against the direction of motion, so without a continuous push the cycle stops.

quiz.q: By Newton's first law, an object in motion continues moving with
options: Constant velocity unless a net force acts on it
quiz.why: The first law says a moving object continues with constant velocity unless a net force acts.

quiz.q: A person pushes a moving box forward with a force exactly equal to the friction on it. The box will
quiz.why: Equal and opposite forces balance, net force is zero, so by the first law velocity stays constant.

quiz.q: An object moves with a constant velocity. The net force on it is
quiz.why: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the net force acting on it is zero.

quiz.q: A net force changes an object's velocity. This change in velocity is called
quiz.why: A change in velocity means the object is accelerating, so a force produces acceleration.

quiz.q: In Activity 6.3, what makes the thread pull the cart with a constant force?
options: The falling cup pulled by gravity
quiz.why: The cup moves down due to gravity, and the thread pulls the cart with a constant force.

quiz.q: The same net force acts on an empty cart and on a cart loaded to double the mass. The loaded cart's acceleration is
quiz.why: From a = F/m, doubling the mass while keeping the force same halves the acceleration.

quiz.q: You sit on a wheeled chair and push a heavy table away from you. Your chair will
options: Roll backward, away from the table
quiz.why: The table applies a force on you in the opposite direction, so the chair rolls backward.

quiz.q: To move forward on a bicycle without pedalling, you push the ground
quiz.why: Your feet push the ground backward, and the ground pushes your feet forward.

quiz.q: It is difficult to walk on a wet polished floor because
options: The floor pushes you forward too strongly
Friction between your foot and the floor becomes very small
Your feet become lighter on water
The wet floor attracts your feet
quiz.why: With little friction, your foot slips backward instead of the ground pushing you forward.

quiz.q: In the two-box system, the force transmitted through the connecting string is called
quiz.why: The equal and opposite string forces between the boxes are called tension T.

quiz.q: Two boxes joined by a string are pulled by force F. Which force is internal to the system of both boxes?
quiz.why: Tension acts between the two boxes inside the system, so it is an internal force.

quiz.q: Two boxes of masses m1 and m2 are pulled by force F on a frictionless surface. The acceleration of the system is
quiz.why: The system behaves like one object of mass m1 + m2, so a = F/(m1 + m2).

examples.title: Net force from two pushes
examples.problem: Two forces of 10 N and 6 N act on a block lying on a table (Example 6.1). Find the magnitude and direction of the net force when the forces act (a) in the same direction and (b) in opposite directions.
steps: Same direction: the net force is the sum of the magnitudes, 10 N + 6 N = 16 N, acting toward the right side.
Opposite directions: the net force is the difference of the magnitudes, 10 N - 6 N = 4 N.
For opposite forces, the net force points along the force of larger magnitude, here the 10 N force.
examples.answer: 16 N to the right when the forces act together; 4 N along the 10 N force when they oppose each other.

examples.title: Pushing a moving box, first law style
examples.problem: A person exerts a forward force on a moving box that is exactly equal to the force of friction between the box's bottom surface and the floor (Example 6.2). Will the box continue moving or come to rest after some time?
steps: Friction acts on the box in the backward direction.
The forward push and the backward friction are equal and opposite, so they balance each other.
The net force is zero, so by Newton's first law the box's velocity cannot change.
examples.answer: The box continues moving with constant velocity.

examples.title: Graphs when no net force acts
examples.problem: Draw the position-time and velocity-time graphs for an object on which no net force is acting (Example 6.3).
steps: With no net force there are two possibilities: the object is at rest, or it moves with constant velocity.
At rest: the position does not change with time, so the position-time graph is flat, and the velocity stays zero.
Constant velocity: the position-time graph is a straight line, and the velocity-time graph is a flat horizontal line at the constant value.
examples.answer: Rest gives a flat position-time line and a zero velocity line; constant velocity gives a straight rising position-time line and a flat non-zero velocity-time line.

examples.title: Acceleration of a two-box system
examples.problem: Two boxes of masses m1 and m2 rest on a frictionless horizontal surface, connected by a string. A force F pulls Box 1 to the right. Find the acceleration of the system.
steps: Box 1 pulls Box 2 through the string, and by Newton's third law Box 2 pulls back equally; this tension T is an internal force.
Internal forces need not be considered; only external forces matter, and here the only horizontal external force is F.
Treat both boxes and the string as a single object of mass m1 + m2 and apply Newton's second law: a = F/(m1 + m2).
examples.answer: a = F/(m1 + m2), directed along the pull F; the system accelerates like one object of mass m1 + m2.

steps.label: Measure the force
steps.detail: A spring balance reads the magnitude of any force, from weight to a pull.

steps.label: Add up the forces
steps.detail: Forces in the same direction add; opposite forces subtract to give the net force.

steps.label: Check the balance
steps.detail: Balanced forces give zero net force, so nothing changes.

steps.label: Meet friction
steps.detail: Friction opposes motion and must be countered to keep things moving.

steps.label: Apply the first law
steps.detail: Zero net force keeps rest or constant velocity.

steps.label: Apply the second law
steps.detail: A net force gives acceleration in its direction: a = F/m.

steps.label: Apply the third law
steps.detail: Forces come in equal and opposite pairs between two interacting objects.

steps.label: Handle whole systems
steps.detail: Treat connected objects as one mass m1 + m2 driven by external forces only.
